title: Unilateral Exotropia in the Elderly: A Clinical Masterclass
summary: Unilateral exotropia (XT) in older adults is rarely primary; it often signals sensory deprivation, neurogenic decompensation, or mechanical orbital shifts. This guide details the diagnostic pathway from vasculopathic palsies to the 'Sagging Eye' syndrome.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Classification
sections.content: Unilateral Exotropia in the elderly refers to a constant or intermittent outward deviation of one eye. Unlike childhood strabismus, adult-onset XT is frequently secondary. It is classified into Sensory XT (vision loss in one eye), Consecutive XT (post-esotropia surgery), and Paralytic XT (nerve palsy).

sections.title: Sensory Exotropia: The Most Common Cause
content: Defined as XT resulting from unilateral visual impairment.
Mechanism: Loss of fusion reflexes leads to the eye seeking a position of rest (usually abduction in adults).
Common triggers: Dense nuclear sclerotic cataract.
Advanced Age-Related Macular Degeneration (wet or dry).
Chronic Retinal Detachment or Vitreous Hemorrhage.
Unilateral Glaucoma with severe field loss.
Corneal scarring (e.g., post-Herpetic).

sections.title: Emergency Warning Signs (Red Flags)
content: Sudden onset XT with an enlarged, non-reactive pupil (Aneurysm risk).
New onset XT accompanied by severe 'Thunderclap' headache.
XT with associated proptosis or chemosis (Carotid-Cavernous Fistula).
Variability of XT throughout the day with ptosis (Myasthenia Gravis crisis).
Bilateral involvement or 'Crossed' signs (Brainstem stroke).

sections.title: Neuromuscular: Ocular Myasthenia Gravis
content: The 'Great Mimicker': Can present as any pattern of strabismus.
Diurnal Variation: XT worse in the evening or with fatigue.
Cogan's Lid Twitch: Overshoot of the eyelid on upgaze.
Fatigability: XT increases during prolonged upgaze or reading.
Ice Test: Improvement of ptosis/alignment with cold application.

sections.title: The 'Sagging Eye' Syndrome
sections.content: A mechanical cause of strabismus in the elderly due to involutional degeneration of the Lateral Rectus-Superior Rectus (LR-SR) band. While it typically causes divergence insufficiency (Esotropia), it can manifest as a cyclovertical deviation or 'Heavy Eye' XT in high myopes, where the globe herniates through the muscle cone.

sections.title: Essential Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Visual Acuity & Refraction (Rule out sensory cause/anisometropia).
Step 2: Prism Cover Test (Measure at distance, near, and in 9 cardinal positions).
Step 3: Ductions & Versions (Check for limitation suggestive of palsy or restriction).
Step 4: Slit Lamp & Fundoscopy (Identify cataract, AMD, or optic nerve pathology).
Step 5: Pupil Assessment (Crucial for CN III palsy differentiation).
Step 6: Specialized Tests (Ice test for MG, Forced Duction for mechanical restriction).
Step 7: Imaging (MRI Brain/Orbits if neurogenic or orbital etiology suspected).

sections.title: Surgical Management Protocol
content: 1. Establish Sensory Potential: Determine if the patient has fusion or if they will suppress.
2. Prism Adaptation: Trial prisms pre-operatively to assess risk of post-op diplopia.
3. Muscle Selection: Usually Lateral Rectus Recession + Medial Rectus Resection (R&R) on the non-dominant/blind eye.
4. Adjustable Sutures: Highly recommended in elderly to fine-tune alignment on Day 1.
5. Post-Operative Monitoring: Watch for consecutive esotropia in the early weeks.

content.explanation: S: Secondary to cataract; E: Exotropia (Consecutive); N: Nerve Palsy (CN III); S: Sagging Eye; O: Ocular Myasthenia; R: Retinal disease (AMD); Y: Young-at-heart (Decompensated childhood XT).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always check for a 'Reverse' Binocularity (Horror Fusionis) before surgery in adults.
Vasculopathic CN III palsies usually resolve spontaneously within 90 days.
In sensory XT, the eye with poorer vision usually deviates outward in adults, whereas children may develop esotropia.
Adjustable sutures are the gold standard for adult strabismus surgery to account for variable muscle tone.
